speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the expressions used yesterday by his representative in London, the High Commissioner for Canada, in speaking-I assume of hon. members of this house-and of the judiciary of Canada in a manner which I regard as casting a reflection upon both. I am quoting from the Canadian Press cable despatch from London yesterday:
Hon. Mr. Ferguson spoke of the question of appeals to the privy council as provided by the British North America Act.

Canadian High Commissioner
Then in quotations:
"Sometimes we have heard from men of short vision and small caliber that we have the brains in Canada to decide such questions of appeal."
All that is within quotation marks in the despatch. My right hon. friend will recall that yesterday this house was discussing that very question. I do not think that the hon. members who took part in the debate were either of "short vision" or "small caliber;" I think they were very fair representatives of the people of this country. I submit that the remarks of the high commissioner are not only a reflection upon those who hold views favourable to discontinuing appeals to the privy council, but are also, in the manner in which they are expressed, a distinct reflection upon the judiciary of this country. I do not see why Canada's position on any matter should be presented to the British public by its representative in London in language of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no reason to know whether the report referred to is accurate or inaccurate.

subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext: It would be accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext: How does the hon. gentler man know?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext:
I cannot think hon. gentlemen opposite have any larger means of knowledge than I have in that regard. But this I will say: I have received several communications recently and I doubt not that some hon. members have seen an article which appeared in an English paper, wondering exactly why it was that so many people in Canada, but not elsewhere, were directing attention to the speeches of the High Commissioner for Canada in London. It would seem, as the despatch indicated, that they seize upon some particular paragraph or sentence unrelated to the text, and from that endeavour to make it appear that the utterances of the high commissioner, are out of line with Canadian sentiment. Be, that as it may, I do state with certainty that he is filling his duties with .great acceptance to the people of England, as is indicated not only by the very large number of communications which have come to me since, the attacks were made upon him in this house, but also by the public press itself. In view of the fact that in so many instances unrelated sections of his addresses have been seized upon, I should have to be satisfied definitely not only as to the accuracy of the report just read by the right hon. gentleman but also as to how and when it was said.
As I indicated some days ago, in matters of this kind very frequently observations
have been made in a jocular sense, but when they appear in print they seem very serious indeed. That has happened on more than one occasion and to more than one public man, for the reason that in a printed speech you cannot get the inflection of the voice, nor can you reproduce the facial expression as the words were uttered, so that in many instances what seemed to be nothing more than a passing joke has been taken as a serious declaration or statement because of that inability to translate the jocular into cold print. For instance, I know of hon. gentlemen in this house who have made observations which seemed very amusing at the moment, but when they were read in Hansard it was somewhat difficult to find exactly where the humour was. So I have no doubt that in many instances the remarks which have been attributed to the high commissioner

and one in particular which is recalled to my memory at the moment-have been made in a jocular way and were not intended to be treated seriously. At public gatherings I have heard distinguished public men of this country call some of their friends men of small vision and small calibre, knowing that the men to whom they spoke were opposed to their viewpoints. It seemed to them an amusing incident, as they passed on. That happens frequently; I have seen it happen at meetings of the Canadian Bar Association and other gatherings of that kind, and I am bound to say that I have known it to happen even in this chamber.
So perhaps under the circumstances the right hon. gentleman will conclude that he is somewhat in error in thinking that the high commissioner for Canada is endeavouring in any sense to cast aspersions upon the judiciary of this country, because I notice this sentence did not end where the hon. gentleman ended it, but went on to say something further as to the reason why this attitude of mind sometimes was to be deplored. For my own part 1 have always felt that the value of an appeal to the privy council was that we escaped the possibility of dissenting judgment, in that a single opinion is given in the advice tendered to His Majesty, which has had a most beneficial effect upon the construction of our constitution and the body of jurisprudence which has been created by those opinions and judgments. Everyone in the legal profession is well aware that great difficulties have arisen from the various opinions which have been expressed in our own courts with respect to the construction of our constitution. When it has been crystallized into a single opinion, and the jurisprudence has been built up from precedent to precedent, each case taking full

Canadian High Commissioner
cognizance of the case which preceded it, we have as a result a body of jurisprudence in connection with the interpretation to be given sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act which, in my humble judgment, it would have been quite impossible to create if there had been no court of appeal such as this. Whether or not the time has arrived when this practice should cease it is not for me to say at the moment, but I do say to my right hon. friend that I am satisfied that any observations made by the high commissioner were not meant in any sense to reflect either upon the capacity or ability of his fellow Canadians or upon their judicial qualities. I think that may be taken for granted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext: My right hon. friend is entitled to express any views he may have with respect to appeals to the privy council, but I ask him whether he thinks the high commissioner for Canada, speaking in public, should deal at all with that question except under instructions from the Prime Minister, for which the Prime Minister must take full responsibility?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DOMINION DAY SPEECH AS CABLED TO CAN.AD IAN PRESS
speechtext: I am bound to say, Mr. Speaker, that I have never heard of any government instructing its high commissioner to make a public statement of that kind on Dominion day. It is certain that Lord Strath-cona did not do so in any of the addresses I heard him make, and certainly the predecessor of Mr. Ferguson would not have made such observations under instructions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 106, to amend the Special War Revenue Act.
He said: I do not know whether it was intended to indulge in any debate upon this measure at the moment; I thought probably

it was placed upon the order paper in order that the bill might receive its second reading to-day. Several suggestions were made when the resolutions were being considered in committee, and to one or two of them effect will be given as the measure progresses. I do not know that I can usefully add anything at this stage to what was said yesterday, and therefore I move the second reading.

Does my
right hon. friend intend to amend the bill in committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Effect will be given to the suggestion of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Cayley) dealing with the question of mutual insurance companies, and to the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Gray (Mr. Porteous) with regard to the definition of the word "company." Then it is proposed to give effect to the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) with respect to goods valued at $25 or less being free from excise tax when brought into Canada by persons entering this country, whether tourists or otherwise. I think there is also one clerical error to be corrected.
What about the stamp on cheques under $5?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That has not been decided.

I do not want to delay this measure, but since I kept perfectly silent during the budget debate and during the debate in committee with regard to the resolutions, I just want to set forth my objections to the main provisions of this bill.
I cannot but deeply regret that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to give expression in legislation to what he proposed some years ago: that instead of dealing with matters of consumption taxes by way of sales tax, he has not elaborated the plan of a turnover tax, which would have given a much better result as far as the public exchequer is concerned, while it would have enabled the people to know just what they paid. My objection to the sales tax is that the consumers really do not know what they pay, and I well remember the hon. gentleman quoting an expression of that old authority on matters of taxation, Adam Smith, to show that one of the main features which should accompany all forms of taxation is visibility.
Then I have a word to say with regard to the so-called excise tax of one per cent. Having regard to the present conditions of the

Special War Revenue Act
country I have not much objection to the rate, but what was stated yesterday is perfectly correct. This tax should come out under its true name; it is a customs duty over and above such duties as are provided in the tariff. An excise duty is essentially a tax levied by the government upon goods produced and consumed in the country, and any tax levied upon imported goods is a customs duty.
But these are small things. My main objection concerns the stamp tax and some of the exemptions from taxation in connection with the transfer of titles. There was a good deal of discussion last night with regard to the stamp tax on cheques; but I was surprised that among so many practical men of business who took part in it, none suggested the very simple method of having the banks become the tax collectors. Every cheque issued upon which a stamp is supposed to be placed eventually comes to be cashed at the bank upon which it is drawn, and if the tax were levied by the bank and charged to the issuer of the cheque, it would do away entirely with the stamp, postage or excise, and the collection would be made by the government from the bank. Suppose a man issues 50 cheques a day: they go either directly to the bank in which the company or individual has an account, or they go through the clearing house. But they all finally reach the bank on which they are drawn; and as every one of those cheques came in, the bank would affix the stamp and add its value to that of the cheque. Each evening the bank could ascertain how much it owed the government in connection with all cheques cashed during the day. Moreover, the power of supervision on the part of the government would be quite easily exercised because the banks keep all cheques for several weeks and sometimes months.
The point made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) is well taken. If people use postage stamps instead of excise stamps then the government will lose 50 per cent of the tax. I have no objection to the postmasters getting a little benefit, but not in this way. This tax is supposed to be imposed for the full benefit of the country, and I have an objection to the taxpayers of Canada contributing in any indirect way to an increase in the salaries of postmasters, with the result that the country loses the whole surplus taxation which is intended to remedy the present condition of the exchequer.
With regard to small cheques, the suggestion made to exempt cheques up to $5 is a
good one. But as to the tax itself, the government was right in coming back to further taxation on cheques small and large.
With regard to the point made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), that there should be a difference in taxation according to the amount of the cheque issued, there is ground for discussion. But if the method I suggest were adopted it would be quite easy for the government to see, through the banks, that cheques from $5 up to SI 90 paid the 2 cents, cheques from $100 to $200, 4 cents, and so on. That is in the hands of the government ; but in regard to the so-called nuisance of this form of taxation, instead of substituting postage stamps for the excise stamp, as a result of which the government stands to lose one half of the returns, it would be far more practical, from the point of view both of the government and of the taxpayers, to do away with the stamp on cheques. If that were done, I come back to the suggestion I made to the former government. If the banks were charged with the responsibility of taking the 2 cents from every cheque issued, then I submit that we should extend this principle and oblige the banks to levy 2 cents on every coupon presented at their offices for collection. I have discussed the matter with some of the most reliable accountants in Montreal, men of high responsibility whose names, of course, I cannot divulge; and they have assured me that the treasury of this country loses hundreds of thousands of dollars every year in connection with the income tax by reason of the evasion by debenture holders of the tax on coupons.
We always take as our examples England or the United States, although I notice that this government has a tendency to copy more exclusively the methods of the United States. But we should enlarge our views and study the conditions that exist in countries other than the so-called English-speaking countries. Take Italy. She was at one time on the verge of bankruptcy-in fact, she was bankrupt at the end of the war. Perhaps the most efficient statesman whom that kingdom has known since it completed its unity in 1870, Signor Giolitti, was struck by the amount of revenue lost by the state in connection with debentures issued either .by the government or by private companies. He had a law passed which Obliged both the government and companies to issue nothing but debentures payable to the creditor, which required the presentation of every debenture with its coupons at certain offices. By this means the revenues of Italy on that account were nearly doubled, and,
Special War Revenue Act

besides, it greatly diminished what the Prime Minister has so reasonably denounced as one of the -causes -of the present crisis, namely, stock gambling, a folly which has wrought so much evil in this country.
I regret that, either with a view to public economy or to increase the revenues of the country, the government has not endeavoured to find means of taxing stock gambling operations. If they cannot put a stop to the practice, at least the country should get some benefit from it. I would; far rather see it stopped altogether and stock gambling made a crime, because it is certainly much more criminal, much more injurious to the social and economic safety of the country, than many of the things which by statute we have made criminal in the past.
I reserve for another -occasion the observations I have to make with regard to income tax. But I think it is regrettable that in its honest endeavour to improve the financial conditions of the country the government has not adopted more energetic methods of dealing with the situation. Let me say at once that I appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister has faced that situation with a measure of courage and energy which we can all admire. We may differ from his policies, but in this regard he is entitled to a tribute of admiration from every Canadian citizen. My only -regret is that he has set aside his best ideas to adopt what I consider to be a weak method of dealing with the situation. For a great number of years, this has been to a large extent the curse both of the social and of the economic situation in Canada. We are faced with the influence of men who are, to bom-ow the words attributed to our representative in London, men of small vision. They may be great captains of industry, they may be manipulators of millions and hundreds of millions of dollars, but they have not the proper sense of social and economic equilibrium.
In all these matters the duty of the government is not only to consider the views of the banker, the views of the trader, the views of the manufacturer; they should consider, first, the general interest of the country, including all classes, but especially the poorer classes; second, they should consider the exigencies of the public purse, and, third, the peculiar interests or claims of this or that class of the puiblic. Unfortunately for many years ou-r fiscal policy has -been framed alternatively by this or that class, .by industry or finance, and very seldom has a study been made of all economic and social viewpoints. The same tendency shows itself with a vengeance, in these proposals. I will not for the moment

refer to the other features of the budget which have no -reference to this bill, but when the income tax and the amendments to the tariff are before the committee I may have something more to say. At the present time I simply state that I cannot agree with the main dispositions of this bill because in my opinion they do not fit the situation, because they will not apportion fairly the load of new taxes upon all classes of the community, because they will not give to the government the amount of revenue-I will not say to which it is entitled;-which it is bound to collect if we are going to preserve the credit of Canad-a.
We should not be deluded. I am not a pessimist, nor an optimist. Statesmen, all men responsible for the welfare of the country, should be realists and see things as they are. The situation may not be desperate but it is very bad. For many months the Prime Minister has attempted to show a spirit of optimism, but yesterday his conscience and sense of duty imposed upon him the painful task of depicting the situation in far darker words than those used by any hon. member of the opposition or any independent individual in this country. We have a very serious situation to meet, serious as far as the finances of the country are concerned, serious as far as maintaining the credit of the country is concerned. The provinces, the private and corporate enterprises, every one, will have need during the months to come of the credit of Canada. After all, the credit of the various provinces, the credit of the various industries and the credit of all individuals at large is, in the long run, governed by the credit of the country, and reversely the credit of the country is affected by the economic condition of the various units, political, industrial or other, which compose the whole of the tax paying community of Canada. If we want to maintain the credit of Canada and thereby the credit of the provinces; if we want to help the sufferings of a vastly increasing number of Canadians, we should see that every measure adapted by this government to derive revenue, to put money in the coffers of the country, for the benefit of the community at large, should give to the country all that it is entitled to. This should not be lost or cramped, through various small avenues, by such means as the use of postage stamps instead of excise stamps. This should have been made the occasion for the enlarging of the basis of our direct taxation in order to increase the revenues of the country by reaching those sources of income which are not at present reached either because of legal

Special War Revenue Act
evasion or the dishonesty of the ratepayer. Such dishonesty is favoured by the dispositions of our present fiscal laws. This applies to most forms of taxation, but especially to the income tax.
This would have been the proper time to have applied those great principles which no hon. member has presented to this house as did the Prime Minister himself. I think it was in 1928, that he criticized the budget of that year in what I consider to have been one of the most thoughtful and masterly addresses on matters of finance and taxation ever given in this parliament. Surely it is not through lack of courage, surely it is not because his authority in the government is not strong enough, surely it is not because he is not master of his administration, that this is not done. What are the causes? Why has not the Prime Minister at this present juncture, with the courage he has evineed so far, taken perhaps the one occasion which will be afforded in his whole life of putting into force and of enacting into law those great principles of taxation which he enunciated three years ago? I deeply regret that he has not done so. I regret it for the country's sake, and I regret it for the sake of the right hon. gentleman himself, because whether or not we differ with him, every hon. member will agree that in the interest of the country every statesman who is loaded with the responsibility of ruling it should do so in the most capable manner, and should be permitted to do so without being impeded by petty party obstacles or sordid interests. The right hon. gentleman knows that when I say this, I say it as a sincere Canadian. I may have more inclination for one party than the other; but long ago have I ceased to consider this or any question from a party viewpoint.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
from the discussion which has taken place on the resolution it must be apparent that the opposition entertains very strong objections to many features of the bill now before the house, which bill is based on the resolution. Were circumstances other than what they are with respect to the stage reached in the present session, and the amount of work which still remains to be done, we would avail ourselves of the opportunity which the second reading of this bill affords us to repeat with emphasis many of the objections which have already been put forward. However, as long as it is understood that our objections have in the main been voiced by what has been said on the resolution, and recognizing as we
must that the government by its majority will carry the measure anyway, we will refrain from further protest and cooperate with the government in expediting the remaining business of the session which includes, of course, the measure which is now before us.
Having listened with great care to the speech which has just been delivered by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I do not hesitate to say that he has expressed in a clear way what is uppermost in our minds with respect to the taxes which are to be imposed under this particular measure. In a word, we feel that the administration has not taken sufficient account of what is known as the incidence of taxation. In imposing new taxes they have not considered sufficiently whether the outcome of the taxation will be to relieve burdens where there is great need of burdens being relieved, nor have they sufficiently endeavoured not to increase the burdens of those who are already bearing as much as they are able to bear in the way of taxation. My right hon. friend has not considered sufficiently whether or not those who are best able to meet the obligations of the state through taxation should at a time like this bear a larger share of the burden of taxation, or at all events he has not prepared his legislation along those lines. That, in a word, expresses our views with regard to many of the features of the present bill.
May I say that if the resolutions had remained as they were presented, we would have had occasion to take much stronger exception to the taxation proposed even than we do at the moment. One of the great objections to the measures my right hon. friend has introduced has been the rough and ready and wholesale manner in which he has sought to deal with everything he has touched in the way of taxation. If he had been a little more restrained in making changes at the beginning of his term of office; if he had had more regard for the fact that previous governments had also wrestled with this question of taxation and that all existing taxes have been the result of long and careful study, not only by previous administrations, but also by the House of Commons in the many discussions which have taken place here he would have seen the wisdom of continuing more in accord with the forms and provisions of taxation which he found upon the statutes. To make clear one great change, my right hon. friend in the resolutions as introduced swept aside with a stroke of his pen, all the exemptions that had been made under the sales tax.

In one part of Mr. Tovell's letter he refers to certain conditions that prevail in the west that make it necessary, or at least desirable, to issue a cheque for every can of cream that is sent to the creamery. The situation in the east is I think generally that of paying semi-monthly or monthly. The condition in the west means a very large number of cheques and Mr. Tovell in the closing paragraph of his letter makes this statement:
Using our own Dauphin plant as an illustration, we are issuing at the present time about 1,600 cream cash tickets a week; using this as a basis, you can readily compute what this stamp is likely to cost us in a year; my own estimate is that the stamp on cream cash tickets will cost our three plants somewhere between $4,000 and $6,000 per year, and as you are undoubtedly aware, there is only one place

where this can come from and that is out of the proceeds which would otherwise go to the farmer. It seems to me that dairying in its present condition will be adversely influenced by this tax.
The above may not he news to you, but on ihe other hand it may possibly bring the seriousness of the matter a little more clearly before you.
At a time when agriculture requires all the assistance possible, this particular question, although it may seem small, might receive a little further consideration.

1
have just a word to say in comment on the remarks of my deskmate, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). He expressed my sentiments so much better than I could have done, there is no need for me to elaborate except in regard to one point. He alluded to the fact-and it is I believe a welll known fact-how largely men of more or less wealth, possessors of bearer bonds with coupons attached, evade their responsibilities toward the income tax by clipping those coupons at the bank so that there is no record of them and they do not make any return of them in their income tax returns. Some comments have been made in the press that now that people have to convert those bonds under the recent legislation, they are being, so to speak, checked up, as proving they possess a large amount of money in bonds, a record of which has not been shown in their income tax returns. It is in connection with the remarks of my hon. friend on that point that I want to make one comment. He suggests the remedy would be to have the government impose a tax of one or two cents on each of those coupons and have the bank collect it as they are cashed. That has two objections, or one at least: it would involve the payment of an income, tax by people who have quite small means, whose total income would come far below the exemption allowed by law. So as long as they cashed those coupons, sometimes for small amounts, such as $1.38 and so on, they would be paying an income tax which according to our law they are not supposed to do. I would suggest this could be got over by the method adopted in Britain. There, on every coupon of that description, the income tax is calculated and collected by the bank If there are any people-and there are thousands of them-whose total income would come within the exemption, it becomes their duty to make an affidavit annually of what reductions have been made from their coupons in that regard, and the government then returns the amount. This method has been proved to work satisfactorily and with no great hardship. No one is going to complain very much

Special War Revenue Act
if he is compelled once, a year to make out a form which will give him a repayment of income tax, and this method contains the much-desired feature that those who have the income will pay the income tax which they are supposed to do and which under our present system it. is so easy to avoid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am compelled to make just two or three observations in closing the debate on the motion for the second reading of this measure. I wonder if the hon. member for Lafoelle realizes that I feel just as he does. I have very strong and well defined views with respect to taxation. I expressed them to the house some years ago, and I was attacked very bitterly in the press of the country because I had done so. I was rather amused to hear my hon. friend's suggestion that the basis of taxation should be broadened so that every man should make a contribution to the state-
According to his means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-according to his ability, and then to hear the observations of my right hon. friend opposite with respect to following all the forms of taxation that had been provided by previous adininistrations. If on the one hand we are to follow what has been done, then you have the result which we have; if you are to blaze a new path and make a new road with respect to taxation, you must drastically alter your methods. In other words, you cannot make an omelette without breaking eggs.
What happened in this country is well known. Last spring as soon as it became apparent that it would be necessary to provide for additional taxation to balance the budget there was carried on from one end of Canada to the other a campaign against a turnover tax. I was flooded with memorials from various parts of the country, the origin of which I well knew. The turnover tax was not a success when in recent years it was first tried in France. It has, however, become a very great success. It takes time to accustom the people to it, and in my judgment therefore it followed that having regard to economic conditions and the very great difficulties which were to be experienced in this country in all forms of industry it was unwise to try a new form of taxation, and very desirable as little as possible to dislocate the business of the country. To my mind it was desirable to secure the money required by recourse to well known and practised forms of taxation rather than to break into new ground with a turnover tax. That is the reason hon. members are not asked to
consider in this house a turnover tax. I believe my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) was sincere in his suggestion with regard to taxation, because on more than one occasion he has done me the honour to talk about the matter privately. Probably he will realize that the disappointment to me is far greater than it can be to him and in fact greater to me than to any other hon. member. Realizing those facts he will appreciate my position. I should like to have seen applied in Canada some new system of taxation, and he is quite right when he says it is not at all probable that I shall ever have a chance to try a new form of taxation, because it is not at all likely that I shall ever again submit ways and means to this house. I am not without hope, however, that some Minister of Finance reviewing the means by which taxes may be raised will realize the values and benefits accruing from a turnover tax.
What I placed upon Hansard three years ago represented my considered views. The turnover tax would be one upon a professional man's turnover, whether he be a lawyer, a doctor or a dentist. The tax would apply to the rich and poor relatively, the turnover of one being restricted and that of the other being large. The turnover tax on business would obviate the necessity for an income tax with all its difficulties of administration and would come regularly to the country once every month, being paid by all forms of business men in every walk of human life and avenue of effort. In the end I believe this particular form of taxation would be acceptable to the Canadian people. However, as I have said, at the beginning of this year the press and public men throughout Canada began to spread propaganda. I saw it begin and swell, and I saw it begin to take root amongst the people of the country who probably may have thought that this indicated a design in the mind of the minister to impose upon them a form of taxation about which they knew nothing and something which would work great hardship upon them. I took the trouble during my investigation with respect to taxation to secure from France a complete record of their experience with reference to the turnover tax.
I remember being in France when the so-called luxury tax was tried, and I well remember how anxious the merchants were at once to notify a customer that if he came from the other side of the channel he did not need to worry about paying the tax because the goods would be sent to him over there and the tax in that way could be avoided. I remember that that was the first
Special War Revenue Act

thing told to a prospective customer who dealt in the shops. To my mind that action on the part of the merchants indicated that the luxury tax was not working successfully and, as I have said, in the end they had recourse to the turnover tax.
Sir, it has not been my privilege to introduce any new forms of taxation to this country at this time. I do not for a single moment disguise the fact that I would like to have done so. I should like to have written a budget which would have expressed my views with respect to taxation in Canada. That privilege has not been given, and it never will ibe. I do say however that the exemption list in the sales tax is notoriously too large. There is not an hon. member in this house who, when he reads page after page of exemptions, does not realize that in a large sense they have been forced upon the House of Commons by the pressure of politics by both parties-not foy one, but by both. When the original resolutions were offered to this house and the list of exemptions was so limited it was apparent there might be a wider distribution of the area of taxation, and that those who were able to make some contribution to the state would do so. The representations made to the Department of Finance however were these, that we have already this system established and to use the language of my right hon. friend-"It has been riveted upon us." Knowing the forms of taxation and the exemptions, having the forms printed and ready, it was felt that to continue the status quo would be most desirable. That is a conservative state of mind which no Conservative Prime Minister could afford to disregard. It was at once apparent that that faculty or habit of thought which finds expression in the words, "I do not want a new system; I want to stick to what is, because I know what it is," is noteworthy in connection with taxation. No one knows better than those who have endeavoured to raise money by the application of systems and forms of taxation that there is that inertia to overcome on the part of the taxpayer. Obviously the doctrine I have just stated is most conservative and in this instance it is directly advocated by our Liberal friends. It is perhaps one of the passing phases of our civilization that those who are of a conservative bent of thought should follow the maxim that:
That man's the true Conservative
Who lops the moulder'd branch away.
There are many mouldered branches with respect to our system of taxation.
I have made these observations because I share even to a greater degree than does my

hon. friend from La.belle the regrets that we have not been able to give effect to measures which I believe would have been of lasting *benefit to the country. However economic conditions and pressure of events being as they were, coupled with the fact that propaganda. had been carried on in a large way, I regarded it as my duty to maintain the two principles-first, to dislocate as little as possible the business of this country, and secondly to disturb as little as possible existing methods of taxation-to accomplish the end we had in mind, the raising of larger revenues.
There are other matters to which reference has been made which will come up during the passage of the bill through committee. I avail myself of this opportunity however at once to indicate to my right hon. friend opposite my appreciation of the attitude taken by himself and his party, knowing as I do that they are not-Shall I say "wedded" to this measure, but have expressed themselves in committee as being opposed to it in a large way. On the second reading they have fulfilled their duty by making their statements, and I presume on division the bill will go into committee.
I am not unmindful of the observations which have been made by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). I would point out to him that the payment of $4,000 for cream cheques, or $6,000, as he mentioned, would mean an issue of 300,000 cheques or 1,000 per day, if we take a 300-day year. That would mean that nearly two cheques a minute would have to be written by the creameries to which he has referred. Sometimes I find there is a tendency to think that a tax, small though it may be, will impose a greater hardship than in fact it does impose. When the bill is in committee I shall point out to my hon. friend a desire not at this time to press upon cooperative enterprises an undue burden. At the same time however for reasons I have already mentioned I think it not undesirable that some contribution should be made by all the people to the revenue of the country. There is also this to be said, which I suppose has been in the mind of many hon. members. The cheque has taken the place of the receipt, and some time ago if a receipt were written it was the practice to place a stamp upon it. When that was abolished, the cheque of course was treated as a receipt and no stamp was placed upon it if it was less than $10. However, we will, as I have said, have some further discussion on that as it goes into committee. I can only add that a very earnest endeavour has been made by every member of the govern-

ment to have regard to existing economic conditions in Canada, and I shall have some figures to give this house before we dispose of these taxation measures that will perhaps surprise them in their very easy talk of the ability of great corporations, for instance, to pay taxes. It must clearly be within the minds of men, if they take the trouble to acquaint themselves with available information, that during the past year corporations in Canada have had great difficulty to make their income meet their expenditures, having regard to the large fixed charges-with some of which I wholly disagree-and for other reasons which I need not now discuss.

There is hardly a small hamlet without an insurance agent, and these men receive roughly 15 per cent of the premiums from the line companies. They have been losing a great deal of business, amounting to nearly a billion dollars of insurance, to corporations of this class.
Outside corporations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, foreign corporations
not registered in Canada, and therefore no part of the commission on premiums remains in this country. Pressure has been brought to bear-

Is not the
5 per cent tax applicable to foreign companies also?

speechtext: The tax of 5 per cent is now imposed. Then they
would come under the domestic tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
In that case I do not see the force of the suggestion. The 15 per cent tax is for the purpose of bringing companies to Canada, but they may come here and avoid that tax.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Without going into details, some of them perhaps are not register-able under the strict terms of our statutes. A great many people feel, as the hon. member for North Waterloo said, that 15 per cent is a higher rate than might be necessary, so if the committee thinks desirable I am quite content to amend the section in such a way as to place the tax at not less than 5 per cent, the present rate, and not more than 15 per cent, the exact rate to be fixed in the proclamation issued by the governor in council when the statute is brought into operation.
The rate is to be fixed by order in council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I will ask that subsection (d) stand, and the superintendent of insurance will give me the terms in which he would like the amendment.
The other point in connection with this section is that whereas previously the tax was imposed on the net premiums, now it is imposed on the gross premiums.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
And it is to be made retroactive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is not made entirely retroactive; it will not have any force at all until this proclamation is issued.
But it is for the year previous to October, 1931.

speechtext:
For insurance effected or in force on or after the first day of October,
Special War Revenue Act

1931. That is for this fiscal year, as my hon. friend observes. That is hardly retroactive; it is to cover this year.

The section reads:
.... gross premiums payable by such person during the preceding calendar year for such insurance effected or in force on or after the 1st day of October, 1931.
I take it the return would be made in January showing the insurance which was in force in October, premiums on which had been paid in the preceding year, so therefore it is retroactive.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In that sense, it is
the only way in which it could be done. I need hardly say to the committee that these companies are not registered in this country. This is an individual return of payments made to outside corporations on which the tax of 5 per cent is now collected.

Is not this change in the
tax going to place a considerable burden on industries? From information I have received in the past it would appear to me to be almost necessary for some of the industries, in self defence, to adopt this method, because many Canadian insurance companies were charging them very excessive rates and it was almost necessary to secure relief in this way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
These special provisions
of this statute will do something to prevent. a recurrence of that difficulty, and one of the reasons why the statute does not come into force except by proclamation is to ensure that any such situation as that of a monopoly endeavouring to fix excessive rates will be prevented.
In what way will this affect the monopoly that has existed in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This is a large question and perhaps my hon. friend does not desire to enter into any lengthy discussion of it.
I am fully alive to the situation to Which he has directed attention, as I believe preceding ministers of finance have been. That is one of the reasons, in addition to the litigation, why this increased burden will not be imposed except when the act is proclaimed.

I am glad to hear the
Prime Minister say that, but I assure him that there has come to my attention within the past few years evidence that many industries have been charged excessive rates. This mutual insurance scheme in some cases reduced rates to one fourth of what they were previously paying. I certainly think the Prime Minister should be very careful to see [Mr B'mnett.]
that no extra burden will foe imposed until we are sure that industries will not be held up as they have been.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the volume of insurance now in the hands of those affected by this legislation were carried by companies in Canada, the rates would be reduced.
It has been carried heretofore.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The reciprocals always
carry part of it. If the S850,000,000, of which we have knowledge, were in force in companies that are registered in this country the effect would be to reduce the rates, because it represents the very cream of the business, the very best risks, in which the fire hazard is the least. No one knows that better than my hon. friend from South Oxford, because one of his companies, one of the oldest in Canada, did carry some town risks and always found that the best of them were those in connection with which the sprinkler and similar appliances were in use.

Is it not a fact that if the Canadian fire insurance companies had treated our people in Canada right in tjie matter of rates this insurance would never have been written outside? It is because our people were not able to get proper rates from the Canadian fire underwriters that they were compelled to go outside Canada to secure a cheaper method of insurance. We should be careful to see that they are not unfairly dealt with. This is a very drastic increase in the tax placed on this class of insurance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That business has always been written outside.

One of the reasons why
foreign companies could give a cheaper rate than our own companies is that they have no overhead in Canada at all. But why should our companies be called upon to meet a loss because of that fact? There cannot be very much danger of a monopoly when all fire insurance is regulated by the fire underwriters who are appointed for the various provinces of the Dominion to regulate insurance. I have had considerable experience with fire insurance and I know what our people are up against. It was not because they were not getting fair play from the Canadian companies; but the foreign companies, through the mail, were offering rates which they knew our companies could not possibly quote and live, and this simply because they themselves, unregistered in Canada, had no overhead in this country.

Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is not quite correct
to say that the Canadian companies were exploiting our Canadian people. The real truth is that the fire hazard in this country was a very high risk in the early days, with wooden buildings; and fireproof construction only came later in the cities and towns. As buildings became fireproof, with sprinklers and other preventive appliances installed in the buildings themselves, such buildings carried a very special rate, and the business ha3 always gone to institutions carrying that selected class of risk. But as the country has made progress, farm risks have reduced steadily, and in the cities and towns there has been a reduction in risks. When we remember that some of the enterprises to which reference has been made incur no expenses in Canada, my hon. friend will understand that if the business thus lost were retained in Canada it would reduce premiums all round. I assure him that every means that can be taken will be taken to prevent there being any exploitation, and I think the effect of this may be to bring about a substantial reduction in rates on the part of those who are registered in our own country.

On more
than one occasion the Prime Minister promised the hon. member for Macleod and the committee that he would, before bringing this act into operation by proclamation, see that something was done to prevent exploitation. That is largely the point in which we are interested at the moment. I should like the Prime Minister to give the committee something more specific than the assurance that he will do everything in his power to prevent exploitation. I wonder to what extent his powers go in that regard? What provision can he make, or what terms can he enter into? Frankly, I think that the provision in the bill, whether intended to or not, will have the effect of transferring a large amount of business to Canadian companies. That is excellent, providing it does not mean an increase in the premiums now paid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It should mean a decrease.

I should
like the Prime Minister to tell us what he means when he says he will prevent exploitation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. member knows as well as any other hon. member of the house that there is a board of fire underwriters in this country. The hon. member for Macleod has spoken of insurance companies in Canada as a monopoly. I would point out that the measure of premium 22110-210
charged has been fixed after consultation with the fire fighting authorities in the various provinces, recent decisions having placed this matter more largely in the hands of the provinces than heretofore. The conditions imposed with respect to the carrying-on of business in the provinces, especially with regard to taxation, have been very onerous. For instance, since this bill was drafted in the first instance, it has come to our attention that at a recent session of one of our legislatures an additional tax of 5 per cent was imposed on these same companies. A tax of that kind would be prohibitive and would destroy any healthy competition that might otherwise exist. The whole matter has been and is being fully studied by the officials of the department in cooperation with the officials of the provinces and the fire underwriters, who play so large a part in fixing rates upon risks in this country. Unless there is satisfactory evidence that there will be no exploitation of the Canadian insurer, the statute will not be proclaimed.

I do not desire to delay the committee, but I think it is only fair to say that the reason for such a large amount of insurance being carried by these inter-insurance societies is because the underwriters stick to a set of rules in insuring. They seem to follow the same set of rules in insuring every type of building and have not seemed disposed to give the proper rates to many industries which have gone to a lot of expense in order to make their plants as nearly fireproof as possible. Being unable to obtain a proper rate they have to go to some of these inter-insurance societies, mostly organized in the United States, in order to secure some relief in the matter of insurance rates.
They do business here for less than they do it in the United States.

Many of these companies from the United States come into a small town and pick out three or four of the good risks. They insure those risks and will not insure any others. The poorer risks are left for the Canadian companies who have to take the responsibility. That is the reason for their rates being much lower; they have no overhead in Canada.
Should not the man who is the best risk get the best rate?
No doubt he should.

The board of fire underwriters in Canada have laid out a set of rules which are followed regardless of whether a man is a good or bad risk.

Special War Revenue Act

The hon. member in
making a statement like that apparently is not aware of the facts. A great distinction is made between the classes of property, and the rates are based accordingly. If these companies are allowed to come into Canada and take one risk here and another risk in another town, the Canadian companies must take the risks which are left.
The Canadian companies are not compelled to insure any risk. They do just what the hon. member has said the American companies do, they insure the risks they want to insure.
These companies are not all American companies; they come from other countries, such as Lloyds.
I did not suggest they were all American companies; some other hon. member suggested that.

These companies do
business here at rates lower than they are permitted to charge in their own country. They must be licensed and they contribute by means of taxation. Our Canadian companies should be given the benefit of this selective business. If that is done it is anticipated that they will give to the Canadian insurer a lower rate than he has received up to date. Whether or not the hon. gentleman believes in the doctrine of protection, he must realize that the Canadian companies are contributing to the welfare of the country and are paying their portion of the expenses of the country.

There is another feature to this case, these companies do not always pay the losses. I have in mind one particular case where a widow insured with a Canadian company paying the rate of $1.75. Through correspondence with a foreign company she was able to get her insurance at $1.55. She accepted that rate and within two years her house burned down and she never got a cent. This company was not registered in Canada and could not be got at.

I know of a risk taken
with a company located in Maine. An action was taken to recover on the policy in Maine, which was the only place where this company had any assets. The defence raised was that the risk had been taken illegally because the company was not authorized by its charter to carry on business in the province of Quebec, and there was an absolute bar to recovery. I will admit that many of these companies are abundantly solvent and

honour their undertakings, but as the hon. member for Gloucester has seen fit to mention one case, I thought it would be proper to refer to another.

The fire underwriters
classify very extensively and I do not think there is any dispute that excessive rates are charged. They charge rates to cover individual cases and individual hazards. Aside from those companies which subscribe to the board of fire underwriters and are governed by their regulations, there are a great number of countries which do not subscribe and which quote rates promiscuously on individual cases. There is enough competition in this business to ensure that rates will be quoted just low enough to enable these companies to carry on business.

Mr. Chairman, I feel I should say something on this question because it involves, first a principle and, second, individual businesses. I am thoroughly in accord with keeping all the business we can in this country. Canadian companies contribute to our taxes, and so on, but I happen to represent a portion of the country wherein are industries which are of such a type as to find it impossible to pay the regular premiums charged in this country. I refer to the lumbering industry in its various aspects. This is an important industry in the northern part of the province of Ontario, in the province of Quebec and in other provinces of Canada. This matter has come up many times in this house since I have been a member and these companies tell me that it is essential to their life that they be allowed to carry on in what is a form of mutual society, whereby they set their own rates and assume their own risks. I would like to have the assurance of the Prime Minister that these industries will be protected in the future as they have been in the past.

Mr. Chairman, instances
have been given of insurance companies refusing to pay losses, and I would like to know from the Minister, of Finance if it is not possible to penalize such companies and refuse to allow them to do business in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member for Battle River heard what was said with respect to these companies not being registered in Canada. The statement was that we had no jurisdiction over them, they had no assets in this country and there was no way in which we could deal with them.

Could the minister give an answer to my question?

speechtext:

Could these industries

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have already explained -I do not think the hon. gentleman was in his place-that this bill comes into force only upon proclamation, and if there is evidence of the difficulty to which he refers, it will not be proclaimed. Will this apply to companies under provincial or Dominion legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The word "Canadian"
appears in the section. The hon. member is familiar with that conflict of jurisdiction between the provinces and the Dominion which does not seem yet to be settled. We can apparently deal only with companies that are created under Canadian statutes and by authority of this parliament. Perhaps the hon. gentleman has been following these judgments, but it is very uncertain where we stand in defining the relative jurisdiction of the federal parliament and the provincial legislature. We have contented ourselves at the moment with endeavouring to deal only with those enterprises which have their origin either in or under the authority of a statute of this parliament.

The hon. member for
Muskoka-Ontario brought up a point. There are a number of New England mutuals doing business in Canada at a very cheap rate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are not registered.
They have been wonderfully successful.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They handle only
sprinkler risks.

They have been an excellent example to Canadian companies. I understand a number of them are registered in Ontario. I may be wrong in that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I could not answer that question, but I know many of them have not been registered in Canada. The New England mutuals have been among the most successful and best conducted companies in the world. Their activity in connection with industrial matters has been largely in connection with sprinkler risks, and engineers have in every instance visited the premises insured and laid out the requirements on the ground, with the result that their losses have been very small and their success correspondingly great. I do not think they are registered under our act.

I do not know whether
those companies are registered or not, but certainly they are operating in this country and they do not take any risks but sprinkler risks.

They are also doing a
service to the industry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And they are an example.
They are a splendid example to insurance companies in Canada.

It is because they are a
splendid example to Canadian insurance companies I do not like to see any drastic action taken which will drive them out of Canada. As regards this question of taxation, if these outside companies are not paying their fair share of taxation as compared with Canadian enterprises, I do not object to an increase on the rate applicable to them. But we should not endeavour to shut them out of Canada by too drastic taxation.

speechtext:

On section 11-Consumption or sales tax of 4 per cent.

There has not been very much discussion with regard to the rate itself. It seems to have been assumed that the rate will be 4 per cent where it formerly has been one, and the discussion has been directed chiefly to the exemption. No one expects that the Prime Minister will alter this rate; I understand that is the announcement of the government. But in view of the comment made in the course of the debate that people have to pay some sort of stamp tax or make some- such contribution before they are really contributing to the revenues of the state, I wish to read an advertisement which appeared in a newspaper published in my native county only a day or two ago with regard to this stamp tax, for the purpose of indicating to the committee that the people are, at present paying real taxes without having to pay additional taxes through stamps on cheques. The advertisement is as follows:
Recent changes brought down in the federal budget, are sure to mean higher prices on many lines. A sales tax of 4 per cent on everything, and large increases in the duty on certain lines such as tea, canned fruits and vegetables and many others, are bound to bring higher prices. We advise our customers to take advantage of our low prices to-day, and stock up on foods before we have to replace our stock at higher prices.
That is the advertisement, and when I referred yesterday to people looking at their dinner pails this is what I had in mind. It is a definite indication that the people are paying more taxes. Therefore I say we should not consider that people are not doing their patriotic duty if they are forgiven an extra one or two cents in respect of cheques or postage. I am glad to state that since this advertisement was written certain exemptions

Special War Revenue Act
have been restored. In the main however the text of that advertisement is true to-day., and the people of Canada are being taxed largely on food stuffs and clothing.

speechtext:

amendment to this section, that:

speechtext: Whichever is most convenient to the hon. member.

Some years ago I brought to the attention of the late government a situation which existed among small industries in the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick and in portions of northern Ontario where lumbering is carried on. There are small sash and door factories and other factories of that kind operated by only one, two or three men. I have in mind an industry in my own constituency carried on by a father and his son. I pointed out that under the old rate of tax this man and his two sons were making total sales of about $1,800 per year, out of which they had to pay for their materials, maintain their mill and pay the sum of $200 for sales tax. In most cases that money was not got back from the consumers. This type of small, local industry, which in fact has now practically disappeared, by all means should be encouraged. I may add that the small woollen industries could be placed in the same category. To my mind the sales tax should not apply to small concerns which do a business aggregating less than $5,000, let us say, per year. Special consideration should be given to such industries making use of raw material purchased in the immediate vicinity.

In certain other districts furniture is being made by individuals or by small groups. In the constituency I have the honour to represent, in places such as Murray Bay, La Malhaie, Baie St. Paul and Cap a 1'Aigle, there are many people capable of making a set of furniture for a living room or dining room. The work may be carried on by a father and son in a back shop. These people are making their product, probably in the nature of old fashioned furniture, not
Special War Revenue Act

for the open market but for private sale. For instance, my right hon. friend, myself or any other hon. member might decide to go and ask one of those men to design a certain set of furniture. They are carrying on their businesses in a home-like manner and not in a general way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This has reference to what my right hon. friend said a moment ago about allowing a drawback where there was export. In the case of the export of manufactured articles, for example, automobiles and the like, there is very little difficulty in determining what materials have been used and wrought into the article that is being exported; but with respect to exports of the primary industries, for example, of agriculture, mining, lumbering and fishing, I think the committee will see it is going to be very difficult to determine what proportion of any articles imported and used in connection with those industries will go into the exported products and therefore be of a character which will permit of any drawback being made. Last night the hon. member for Hants-Kings, for example, spoke of apples exported from Nova Scotia, and pointed out that fertilizer, spraying machines and other materials and articles had to be imported in connection with their production for export in large quantities. I doubt very much whether it would be possible to assess the cost of the portion of fertilizer and spraying machines entering into the production of exported apples. That is only an example of what will be taking place everywhere when the products of the primary industries are being exported. I do think a tax applied in that way is going to be a real handicap to the export trade of Canada, particularly trade in these primary industries. In yet another way it will affect our manufacturers also. There can be little doubt that the effect of a tax applied to so large a range of imports as this tax is being applied to will be certain sooner or later to increase the cost of living in Canada, and the cost of living increase will be reflected in a demand for an increase of wages, which will be one of the factors entering into the cost of manufacturing and the development of primary industries. To the extent to which the costs of production are increased, the Canadian producer or manufacturer is going to be handicapped in the markets of the world.
I know my right hon. friend desires to find a tax that will make everyone contribute something but whether this is possible or not
all comes back to a due appreciation of the incidence of taxation, which no one knows better than my right hon. friend is the most difficult of all subjects with which political economists have been perplexed. I am certain there would be agreement among political economists that where there are considerable importations, you cannot as is the case at present in Canada, impose customs taxes or an excise tax of any appreciable amount over a wide range and not affect the costs of the materials that enter into manufactured articles and the cost of machinery and implements of production used in manufacture or in the production of commodities and consequently the cost of commodities as well in the great basic industries. I believe this tax is going to prove a real handicap to trade, and that a restriction will be effected in a manner that cannot be remedied, as my right hon. friend suggests, by granting a drawback. This is, moreover, another instance where the primary industries are placed relatively at a disadvantage as compared with manufacturing. As I have said, I believe that with respect to our manufacturing industries you can definitely determine the materials that enter into their manufacture, and to that extent the manufacturer and the industry will get what benefit is to be derived from the drawback; but in these great primary industries of agriculture, mining, fishing and lumbering it will not be possible in the same way to make that determination, and they will be handicapped proportionately.
I should like to draw my right hon. friend's attention to the wording of the section. Something further is required, I think, to bring out his own wish in the matter. After the word "used" in the twenty-seventh line some words should be added which will be broad enough to include not only manufacturing but all the different stages of processing and production "wrought into or attached to articles exported." My right hon. friend will see that after the words "material used," there is nothing to connect those words with the words "articles exported" or to link up the idea with production as contrasted with manufacturing,

(3) Newspapers and periodicals which are required to be transmitted for a greater distance than is mentioned in the last preceding subsection, or the publication of which is of greater frequency than once a week, and the newspapers and periodicals described in the immediately preceding subsection, upon any copies in excess of the circulation of two thousand five hundred copies, shall be subject to postage at the rate of one and one-half

This resolution, as the
committee is no doubt aware, provides for an increase in the rate on newspapers from one cent to one and one-half cents per pound. It may be summarized that with respect to free circulation there is no change; with respect to newspapers and periodicals which are devoted to religion, the sciences or agriculture, there is no change; with respect to newspapers and periodicals other than the above, with a circulation of not more than 10,000 copies per issue, there is no change, and with respect to newspapers and periodicals other than those I have mentioned, with a circulation of over 10,000 copies per issue, the rate will be one and one-half cents per pound.
The hon. member for Gloucester was slightly in error the other night in speaking of this matter. In 1926 the revenue for the carrying of newspapers at the rate of one and one-half cents per pound was $1,290,000. In 1927, when the reduction was made to one cent per pound, the revenue was $966,000, or a decrease of $31,000. The circulation figures involve a consideration of British and foreign papers as well, including those from the United States which, as I thought, are mailed in Canada. It is believed, owing to the exemptions that we have provided in this resolution for country magazines, those devoted to agriculture, science and religion, the probable increase in revenue will be approximately $200,000 or perhaps slightly more. My right hon.
friend did me the honour of commending his observations particularly to myself. I have to thank him for the information he has furnished the committee, not because I did not know about it before, but because thousands of farmers have the same story to tell. After paying out thousands of dollars for wages, for equipment, and for overhead of all kinds they have found themselves with a deficit of $2,090 or $3,000 or more each year. This unsatisfactory condition of affairs applies in a lesser degree to farmers all over Canada. So we can quite understand that men who might be called multi-millionaires, if they have their money invested in corporations that yield no returns, may be paying no taxes at all on suoh investments; they may be exempt because of the losses incurred. I think we all understand that misfortune, and because we do understand it we are the more sympathetic towards those citizens when they are experiencing the same disabilities. I accept my right hon. friend's statement without question. I can quite understand it, because I have been experiencing deficits myself for the last year or two. But I am wondering what prompted him to make an increase n the corporation tax?

speechtext: Surely.
