speechtext: Less than that.

I do not doubt it,
but I was just making a guess, basing it on what I know they paid the year before. What is the use of trying to income tax the fanner? You might as well try to get something in the way of lactic fluid from a cow that had been dry six months or a year as try to get any income taxes from the farmer at the present
time. So I am sympathetic towards the corporations, although it may not be altogether safe to say so. But knowing they are in the same condition as the farmer, why increase their tax? I await my right hon. friend's explanation, and am ready to accept it if it is as good as the other one. I do not think I ever have belonged to any corporations, so that I am quite disinterested, but I should like an explanation for this increase just as I wanted an explanation as to why the farmers should be taxed at this time to any greater extent than they formerly were. So on behalf, if you like, of the corporations of Canada I ask the Minister of Finance why we should impose this extra 2 per cent at this time when so many are already exempt for the lack of anything to tax.

I do not think we should let pass the statement made by the right hon. gentleman a few moments ago without some reflections with regard to the position of the corporations in Canada. I may lack tenderness of heart, 'but there are so many individuals and small concerns suffering in these days that I have not much sympathy left for the corporations. These statements in bulk figures are very imposing, but I think they need some scrutiny.
In the past many of these corporations have disguised enormous profits in various ways. Some have created capital out of profit and distributed shares to their shareholders without those shareholders paying anything for them. I do not think the income tax has ever reached that part of their profits. Corporations have also disguised part of their profits, or rather diminished their margin of profit, in order to create a condition which would appeal to the public for sympathy, by making extraordinary expenditures. A few weeks ago I quoted the instance of the Sun Life Assurance Company, which last year increased its dividends to its shareholders by fifty per cent over the previous year, making the dividend 75 per cent of the apparent capital. I do not suppose there is much watered stock there, but when a corporation is able to pay 75 per cent on the face value of its stock it should not require very much sympathy from hon. members.
This company has put an enormous amount of money into the construction of its new central office, which was entirely uncalled for. Every time I pass that building I cannot but *think that a part of my very small contribution to the building up of that company is invested in that structure. When I took a policy with the Sun Life Assurance Company at the age of twenty-five it was still the
Income War Tax Act

custom of insurance companies to issue a prospectus setting out the type of insurance issued, the amount of the policy, the amount of the premium, the number of years for which it was to be paid, the assessed profits reserved or paid yearly, and the probable profits. When that policy was paid up after twenty years I received the capital and the assessed profits, but of the probable profits I only received half, and of course I knew I was not legally entitled to receive what had been mentioned in the prospectus. One of two things happened; either the operations of the company were well conducted according to their conjectures at the time the contracts were made, or they were not. No one ever suggested that the corporation was not well administered, but what has happened in this case, as in many others, is that the company, to disguise the profits which were accruing from what was paid in by its clients, simply sunk millions of dollars in large buildings such as the one now under construction in Montreal, which will never return two per cent on the capital invested. That capital investment has not been subscribed by the shareholders; as a matter of fact it represents not an investment of capital but rather an amount taken from the profits derived by the company from its insurance business. The same thing may be said of many corporations; 'banks and other financial institutions have followed the same practice, and large industries have invested funds in enterprises not in order to secure revenue but in order to disguise a portion of their profits.
Now, however, the most important question is that of watered stock. I have never been in business in my life, for which I thank heaven every day, especially during times such as these. I do know a few men in business, however, and some time ago I was talking to a man in Montreal who is interested in many things and who has a large business experience. He is a bank director, among other things, but in spite of all that he is an honest man. I pointed out to him the provision in our Companies Act that the issuance of shares for which full value has not been paid to the company is forbidden, and that the distribution of shares except for services rendered is also forbidden. A large part of the watered stock is distributed under the pretence of services rendered. A few gentlemen get together and organize a large company. Let us suppose they are in need of 110,000,000 for the real purposes of the company; they will issue paper for $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 and distribute to themselves a large portion of that paper as paid up stock for which they have not paid one cent into

the coffers of the company. It is distributed to them for services rendered. Then they issue stock at an alluring price to the public, and these shares go up if there are profits or go down if there are not profits. Frequently they go up or down according to the wishes of the directors. If they wish to gather in a large portion of the stock, it goes down on the stock exchange, they purchase it at a low price, and then it goes up again. All these things have to be taken into account.
Would the hon. member be good enough to tell us how that is done?	m

There are many methods. I am not familiar with the details; I am simply giving to the house what has been stated to me by men who are absolutely cognizant of the facts.
Mr. MoGIBBON:	That is not the statement the hon. member made a few moments ago; he made the statement as an absolute fact, but now he says this is what he has been told.

I stated I had gathered the information in conversation with men who are in business and who know all about these operations. In addition, this is a well known fact; any man who has had anything to do with banking or stock exchange operations knows this to be so. I remember some years ago I prepared a whole record for the house with names and everything complete, in order to show the criminal results of stock exchange operations and stock gambling, which is very often conducted by the men who are supposed to be responsible for the good administration of the company concerned.
Then there is another matter. In industrial affairs there is the question of efficiency in management, which is very often neglected for the speculative side of the operation. Mention has been made of salaries. What portion of these salaries is paid to individuals who really work in the company, individuals who take part in what I may call the actual operations of the company? What proportion is paid to the directors for their atendance, and to the president, the vice president, the general managers, who are very often large shareholders, and who draw enormous salaries which are really profits in disguise? All these things have to be taken into consideration. I mention these facts to show that the government is amply justified in raising the tax on the profits of corporations. But what I think should be done in all circumstances, and especially in cir-

Income War Tax Act
cumstances like these, is that a board or an organization of some kind should be established to scrutinize the operations of the company. It should not be left entirely to the companies themselves to present to the government a statement of their affairs for taxation purposes, or to the public for what perhaps I might call deceptive purposes.
The Prime Minister spoke this afternoon about the manner in which the French government had carried out its taxation policy. Of course, in France as elsewhere there is a good deal of speculation and there are many abuses in the conduct of large enterprises. But if -on the whole the economic situation in France to-day is better than it is in any other- country it is because the governments there, with all their political shortcomings, have been much stricter in their supervision of large companies than we have been in this country or in the United States. If there is a danger threatening the economic structure of North America -the United States and Canada are in the same position in this regard-that danger lies in the absolutely loose fashion in which large corporations conduct their business. We have reached the point where we must abandon the old shibboleth of laissez fa-ire, which was perhaps to a certain degree the cause of the great industrial and financial development in England, buit which in the present circumstances, under conditions as they exist in America, with the spirit of speculation rife, which spirit the Prime Minister himselt has so rightly denounced, is a menace to the community. Large corporations have not the right to conduct their business in such a manner. There are some 22,090 corporations in this country, and the way in which so-called private enter-X>rise has been carried on has had more to do with the ups and downs of our economic and financial structure in Canada than the policy of any government can have. I believe that the strict supervision of companies, from the point of view both of the exchequer -and of national stability, is one of the most imperative duties of the government of this [DOT]country.

The Prime Minister was having a little fun -in the remarks he made, and I was having some in return. But I desire to know what his real views are about this increase in the tax on corporations. I will admit that while the Australian treaty economically was absolutely sound, politically it was a mistake to those who were responsible for it. In regard to corporations, will my right hon. friend admit that politically this is good taxation? I should like to have his real 22110-211
opinion as to the advisability economically of taxing corporations of this kind indiscriminately, whether big or little, hard up or well to do.

I say frankly that I have not been able to satisfy myself that the government should set up a department which would give its imprimatur of approval or disapproval with respect to the capital structure of corporations, because it might delude people into believing that, with supervision to that extent on the part of the government, the securities would be necessarily sound. So profound a student as the hon. gentleman, who says frankly that he has no experience in business, for which he is very glad, will realize that in this regard there is a record in other countries. And when the state has endeavoured to scrutinise the capital structures of corporations, and give its approval to the issues of securities, it has sometimes led to very great difficulties. One of them, for instance, arose in this country in connection with a bank, in which there was some contention with respect to the manner in which the provisions of the law were applied. A claim arose, not perhaps enforceable in a court of law, but which this parliament recognized as entitling those interested in one bank, if not in two, to obtain restitution through the aid of the state. This indicates how difficult it would be for the state to undertake generally the duty of supervising the capital structure of issues of securities made by corporations. Undoubtedly, however, there is an increased interest in this country in this regard, and some of the results that have been brought so strikingly and so sadly to the attention of the people of this country during the last fifteen months or two years have made it more and more apparent that the corporate jurisprudence of Canada, which is statutory in form, must be strengthened to protect the people from exploitation.

The Prime Minister would not give me very much information as to the reason for this increase in taxation from 8 to 10 per cent when many people are not paying taxes now because of their poverty.
I think I can prescribe, because he will not do so, a better way of putting some of these business institutions-because that is what they are, after all-on their feet. By giving agriculture, the paramount industry of this country, a better opportunity to get on its feet, is the way to help business to prosper. In addition to agriculture, we have lumbering, fishing, mining, water power development; these five great basic industries should first receive assistance before the business of the country or corporations can show much response.
During the last few months I have been trying to secure a little knowledge of economics. I have been sitting at the feet of some of our economic Gamaliels to my left, and not without some purpose. I have been trying hard to see the advantage of deflating currency. I can see some advantage if we had not to do any buying, but since we have both to buy and to sell, deflated currency is worth just as much less when one comes to buy as it is worth more when one comes to sell, and in this way you are left just where you were. I am willing to sit at the feet of any financial Gamaliel to learn, but I am beginning to wonder whether there are any in this chamber, especially on the government benches, if one may judge by the kind of budget that has been presented and the crawfishing that has had to be done before we can even get started on the resolutions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This item includes administration of sinking fund. Would my right hon. friend tell us when he hopes to be able to introduce a sinking fund provision of which he spoke so often when in opposition?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not so often. I said I believed it was sound financing to provide for a sinking fund, and I have not changed my mind in that regard, but in many countries it has been found necessary to suspend the operation of the sinking fund in times of financial stress. Since William Pitt established it in England, that has been done more than once there and in other countries as well. I assure my right hon. friend that I hope the day may not be too far distant when provision may be made for a sinking fund of respectable proportions. One-half of one per cent has been regarded by many financiers and economists as being reasonable. If we had a fund of $10,000,000 it would make a [DOT] very fair beginning. I am in no better position than is my right hon. friend to say when such a sinking fund will be instituted. Not having been responsible for the revenues of the past year, I can only say it could not well have been established that year, but I can say equally that present conditions do not seem to warrant the hope that it will be established this year.

Is there a grant given to the Red Cross Society?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My memory is that there is no grant to the Red Cross. During the last few years the provinces have made grants to that organization and not the Dominion. The Red Cross occupies a position with relation to war activities of the Dominion, and its peace activities are defined by a statute which brings its operations more nearly within the ambit of provincial legislation. For that reason grants have been made by the provinces. It may be in view of what has transpired during the last few weeks that something will have to be done in that regard.

I made the inquiry because I believe neither the federal nor provincial governments can adequately provide relief for all the destitution which prevails at the present time in western Canada. Some such charitable organization as the Red Cross will have to be called into service, and I am suggesting that they begin operations so that in each town or distributing point clothing and other articles can be collected for distribution during the winter. Not only that, but collections could now be made of goods to be distributed. It seems to me that charitable organizations such as the Red Cross are the right and proper bodies to do the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Apparently the hon.
member is not as familiar with the province of Saskatchewan as I thought he would be. Last year the government of that province granted at first $30,000 and later an additional sum to the Red Cross to care for those requiring clothing and assistance in the stricken areas. So far as I know in every province west of the great lakes there is a provincial Red Cross organization which is responsible for the maintenance of local chapters, as they are called in the United States, or branches, as they are called in Canada. From time to time I receive letters from various branches of the Red Cross in the western provinces. The extent to which we will directly assist the Red Cross has not yet been determined but is receiving our consideration.

The Red Cross did a certain amount of the work last year, but it was very late in the season before they became active, with the result that they were not properly able to look after their work. It is for that reason I now bring the matter
Mr. Bennett.]
to the attention of the government. The Red Cross should become active at once so that they may be prepared to cope with the work thej' will have in hand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Once more may I say that I am surprised my hon. friend from the province of Saskatchewan is not aware of the fact that a permanent provincial organization is maintained in that province. Mr. Kerr I believe was the commissioner for the province, and the activities of the Red Cross have been continuously maintained. If there has been any occasion for criticism, it should be directed to the provincial commissioners and not to the federal government.

While we are discussing
these grants I should like to remind the Minister of Finance that I do not see any item in support of the Canadian Social Hygiene Council. Considering the splendid work they have done, will the government make an appropriation for them in the supplementary estimates? I do not see any item in the main estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no item in
the main estimates. It is apparently an organization carrying on educational work. It has always been believed by the federal government that it is the duty of such government to assist educational organizations of this kind until such time as the results of their work have become apparent in action taken either by the provincial or the federal government, or by both. Due in no small measure to the operations carried on by this voluntary organization, such interest has been aroused as has resulted in practically every province in the Dominion setting up a department of health, and the burden is now borne by the taxpayer. The Dominion has also set up a department of health, the cost of which is also borne by the taxpayer. The sum of $100,000 is voted each year for the various services to which attention has been directed by this voluntary organization. Therefore it is felt the necessity for continuing that form of activity no longer exists.
Is it the intention of the government then to discontinue the grant for the association?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the present view.

May I suggest to the
Prime Minister that the work of this organization is not yet complete. Such educational work must be carried on continually from year to year because, all the time there are people arriving at the age of intelligent

Supply-Finance
thinking who require to have this subject of health brought directly to their attention. To my mind it is most important that this voluntary organization should continue to receive assistance, because all the health activities carried on by the provincial, the municipal and the federal authorities to be effective must have behind them the continued pressure of a well-informed public opinion. Therefore I think the government would be well-advised to reconsider the continuance of this grant.

Supply-Royal Grain Commission

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The Canada Grain Act, including management, operation, maintenance and equipment of elevators, administration of, $2,681,000.

Unfortunately I was absent yesterday, but I understand that during the. day there were some developments in connection with the supplementary appendix to the Stamp commission report. If my hon. friend the minister has anything further to give the committee to-night beyond what developed yesterday we should be very glad to have him lead on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, really I
think everything that profitably can be said on this subject has been said, but we might summarize the situation briefly in this way: The other night when this question was brought before the committee I did not have with me information on the subject. I stated the matter as fully as I could. Last night the Prime Minister dealt with the subject quite exhaustively. I think I can summarize by saying that appendix XII, chart No. 10 as it is termed, was filed with the commission by Mr. Pitblado, counsel for the Winnipeg Grain Exchange; that it was numbered by Sir Josiah Stamp and included in the series of charts and other matters; that it was handed by Sir Joseph Stamp to the secretary of the commission in New York just before Sir Josiah sailed for the old country; that it was brought by the secretary to Ottawa, with the draft report; that the draft report was typed and concluded, as far as its arrangement was concerned, by the secretary and Mr. Sanford Evans, and sent to Sir Josiah Stamp for his revision and final approval.

I should like the
Prime Minister to remain, because I believe he has more information with regard to this matter than the minister has.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
None of the charts of
appendices were sent to Sir Josiah Stamp, because they were not prepared in time for a mail it was desired to catch, and as they had been seen by him already and numbered and passed on by him to the secretary, it was thought unnecessary to forward them. There was no suggestion from Sir Josiah Stamp that he was opposed to the inclusion of this appendix in the report; I understand that he intimated it was one of the appendices he wished included, and it was included with the others. Nothing was changed on it; it was included exactly as it was filed.
With regard to the filing, it should be noted that during the last meeting in Winnipeg,
Mr. Bennett.]
which closed at 12.45, at about 12.20 Mr. Cairns, of the pool, filed a lengthy document, reading parts and leaving it to the commission to peruse the remainder. The evidence discloses that Mr. Pitblado, counsel for the grain exchange, was asked by the chairman if he wished to say anything in regard to this document filed by the pool. Mr. Pitblado replied that he had not seen it before and therefore was not in a position to ask any questions, but he asked for the privilege of filing a chart, which is the chart now before us as appendix XII. That is how it was originally introduced.
Subsequently, when the accuracy of the chart was called in question, the three commissioners were communicated with and they authorized its deletion from the report. This coincided with the indication, to the Prime Minister, to myself and to others as well, of apparent inaccuracies in the chart itself, and therefore further circulation has been stopped. Communications have been sent to all those who received the report, indicating that this particular appendix having been objected to should be deleted and no longer recognized as forming a part of the report carrying the judgment of the commission. I do not know that anything further can be said.
Who requested the removal of appendix XII or chart 10?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As matters stand now, it
has been removed at the request of several persons. The chairman and the two commissioners have agreed to its removal. When the matter was brought to the attention of the Prime Minister he expressed the opinion that it should be removed, and after I had studied the report myself I took the same view. It has been removed accordingly. The point to be borne in mind is this: upon the discovery of the obvious unfairness of the chart it was immediately discarded. I do not know that any more could be done. To those who have received copies of the report- there were quite a number-we have sent out communications indicating that the chart should be removed.

I wanted to find
out whether my hon. friend was prepared to lay down the principle that if any just complaint were made against a report of this kind the government would be justified, after the report had been tabled, in removing the objectionable feature complained about. Take the Turgeon report referred to in the report of this commission, with respect to the question of futures. Let us suppose that Mr. Justice Turgeon, or anyone on his behalf, had com-

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
plained about anything in the Stamp report, whether with respect to exhibits or any other phase of it: would the government be justified in taking such complaint into consideration and eliminating something else from the report? On that principle, where would you end? Is each complaint to be considered and the particular feature of the report objected to eliminated?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a purely hypothetical question, to which my reply is very plain and simple. If it were noted that any inaccuracy had crept into the report, or that there was included in it anything which upon reflection it appeared unwise to retain in the report, and if the commission, those having charge of the matter, considered that it should be removed, it would be perfect!} proper to take prompt action after the circulation of the report with a view to overtaking it. But when my hon. friend speaks of the Turgeon report, made five or six years ago, and uses that as an illustration, suggesting that we should start now to delete any part of that report-

That is not my point. Reference was made in the Stamp re-,port to the 'Turgeon report. Suppose some member of the Turgeon commission were to call the attention of the government to any alleged inaccuracies in the Stamp report, which makes reference to the Turgeon report, is that necessarily a hypothetical case? Would a complaint made by anyone, either a member of the Turgeon commission or anybody else, with respect to the Stamp report, be taken into consideration and the feature objected to deleted? If that principle is sound in one case it is sound all along the line. And I take the ground that it is not sound. There is no justification for it without-obtaining someone's consent. If the government have the right to delete any part of the report, exhibits or anything else, after the report has been tabled, they have the same authority to delete it, or at least to point it out to those who made the mistake, before the report is tabled at all. I took the ground the other night that you could not segregate the various members of the government, which is an entity; for no member is responsible individually. The government is responsible collectively. Now I want to know whether the various members of the government had an opportunity to see the report before it went to the printer, I am concerned to know whether the Minister of Agriculture saw it, because I fancy he would have detected at once the significance of this appendix XII,
inasmuch as he is himself a member of the pool and a contract signer. He would certainly be jealous of the interests of the pool, and if he did not see the report some explanation is called for.

The other night when the matter first came before the house the impression got abroad that someone had dishonestly smuggled that draft into the report, and a demand arose that the guilty party be discovered and punished. Having followed the discussion as it has proceeded, I cannot find anything to persuade me or anyone else that any employee of the government or of the commission was at all culpable in the matter. I suggest to the minister that he see to it that no innocent party is made to suffer.
Mr. STEVENiS: There is no question of that.

I have had the privilege of being in a government for a considerable time both here and in the west, and we have never had a report submitted to us in regard to which the Prime Minister had not invariably consulted his colleagues, to obtain the collective wisdom of the cabinet Every report of importance has been considered by the cabinet as a whole item by item before ever being sent to the printer. This report was heralded throughout the country as one of great importance, and I thought, as I still think, that the personnel of the commission was a first class one. The report itself I do not consider very important, the information having been already known. But what I want to know is whether the report was submitted to the various members of the cabinet, because there is joint and not individual responsibility in connection with this mistake, which is regarded as grave by those who have been adversely affected. I think I have the right, just as the Minister of Agriculture had the right as a contract signer, to get all the information available in connection with the matter. I admit with the hon. member for Weyburn that the situation is different from what it was the other night, because it is now admitted that Sir Josiah Stamp O.K'd the appendix at New York. The fact that the exhibits were not sent back to London for his formal O.K. is neither here nor there, and I would not criticize that point too strongly, although possibly it would have been better so to do. It would constitute a collective responsibility upon the government as to whether or not
3338	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Grain Commission
they looked into this report before they took the responsibility of tabling it. They should have brought the combined knowledge of the cabinet to bear on it with regard to what it meant.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I disagree entirely with
the doctrine set forth by the hon. member.

That of collective
responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, the question of the
reviewing by each minister of the government of all reports which are presented. This is a report made by a commission consisting of three gentlemen, of which Sir Josiah Stamp was the chairman. Hon. members pressed for the early tabling of the report, and as soon as it was received, and as quickly as it was possible for it to be put into proper shape and printed, the Department of External Affairs, under whom the commission had carried on, presented the report. As far as I know the report was not submitted to individual members of the government, and with all due respect to what my hon. friend has said I do not think this has been done under any administration. The government would have no right to change the matter contained in a report, whether it did or did not suit them. Such a report is received as a bona fide expression of the views of the commission submitting it, and we gave to parliament, precisely as we received it, the report of Sir Josiah Stamp.

Would it not have been better to discover the mistake before the report was tabled? If a report is not usually submitted to the whole government, it certainly is submitted to a subcommittee of the cabinet, which makes a report upon it. That is the usual practice, and if it has not been followed out in respect to this report, there would appear to have been serious ministerial neglect. Probably in the hurry to get away Sir Josiah Stamp did not realize the importance of this graph, but it was in the office of the Prime Minister for a month and a half. There were plenty of officers in the department who could have looked over it, and yet I understand that the Prime Minister himself did not read it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not in detail.
Mr. MOTHER WELT,:	A month ago he
said it was his intention to read it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The conclusions, but not the whole document.

I have not read the whole document, but I have read enough to

know what is in it. This chart was in the hands of Mr. Sanford Evans and the secretary of the commission, both very responsible men. I know one of them very well, although I do not know the other. The road was open for it to go right on to the printer without any governmental supervision worthy of the name. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, absolutely.

We have got that
far. It went to the printer and then after it was too late it was found that the damage was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The government had no
right to change that report.

I submit that there is a grave dereliction of ministerial duty in sending on a report like that to the printer without even reading it. Did the Minister of Agriculture have an opportunity of reading this report? Was there an opportunity given to the individual members of the government to see the report before it was printed and tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As far as I know the
report was not submitted to individual members of the government; it was filed with the house as received.

So far as this phase of the vote is concerned I am satisfied, and I believe all parties are satisfied, that the discussion has gone to the extent where we can derive no further profit by prolonging it. We know where the responsibility lies-with the government.
I wish to refer to one further matter in connection with the administration of the grain act. During the last two or three years there has been general satisfaction with its administration, and I should like to see that satisfaction continue. The question of who was responsible for the system of mixing which has been more or less in vogue ever since the year 1912 has come up on more than one occasion, and I think if we could settle that matter now we would be well advised to do so. I would attempt to settle the point, not alone in order to place responsibility but to avoid a recurrence of the abominable system of mixing. During the course of my remarks I shall refer to an order in council which was passed, but I shall blame no one for the passing of it because the measure appeared during war time and may have been passed under the War Measures Act. I refer to order in council No. 2394 which is dated from the Government House at Ottawa, August 25, 1917, a date just previous to the time when the board of grain supervisors got into action. Ostensibly this order in council was put through for the purpose of providing a sample market. For years such a market had been under discussion and many agreed it would be worth having. Although this order in council made the necessary provision, the sample -market never materialized because conditions did not lend themselves to its inauguration. However the mixing which was understood to come into effect with the sample market did take place and became w-orse from year to year until practically every terminal elevator in Canada was engaged in the practice of mixing wheat. As I have said that practice arose through the authority of this order in council passed under the War Measures Act which had for its alleged purpose the establishing of a sample market.
Because of the fact that there was a possibility of greater profits through mixing operations the practice grew and grew until it pervaded the whole country. I am not going to place too severe responsibility, although the practice began in 1917, but I wish to state that the government which preceded this one was blamed for not having sooner abolished the practice, and it is in that
3342	COMMONS
Supply-Royal Grain Commission
connection I make my objection. When a practice such as that of mixing wheat is begun a tremendous effort is required to stop it. When the Turgeon commission we were discussing a few moments ago was appointed in 1923 they brought down a report upon which a bill was drafted by the commissioners and placed before the government and the house. The bill was given a run for its life, and a great many of the safeguards against the evils of mixing eliminated in the agriculture committee. I am blaming no one for that. The fact of the matter was that the government did not have a majority and was not strong enough numerically to have this contentious bill passed in the proper manner. It was brought up again at a time when we had more numerical strength in the house and as a result we have the satisfactory act of to-day, as passed in 1929-30.
Having had that experience I feel competent to state that if this system of mixing ever gets started again it cannot be stopped without still greater difficulty, because forces behind it are so powerful that no government, except one with an enormous majority and a great deal of determination could put a stop to it. If the practice of mixing became prevalent again it would get worse and worse until the Canadian wheat grower would lose his world-wide reputation. At the present time the Board of Grain Commissioners stands behind the act. May I say to the minister that I would be right with him if he made an attempt to stand behind the spirit and terms of the act. I wish to warn him however that if the practice of mixing which was so rampant four or five years ago gets started again, I am satisfied no parliament, without the working of a miracle, would be able to cope with it successfully.
I have taken this opportunity to place the matter before the minister and I make the promise to give my support to any effort on his part to preserve the present anti-mixing law. I believe the spirit of the act has been carried out during the last two years, and I am sure all hon. members on this side of the house would do their utmost to discourage a recurrence of this most unfortunate mixing practice.
I wish to read to the committee one or two paragraphs from the order in council of August 25, 1917, authorizing mixing:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and pursuant to the provisions of subsection 2 of section 57, chapter 27, 2 George V, entitled "The Canada Grain Act," is pleased to approve the following rules and regulations for sample markets, and the same are hereby approved accordingly.

As will be seen from this paragraph the objective was to establish sample markets, and although the establishment never took place, mixing became prevalent. The then deputy minister of justice interpreted the act to mean that inasmuch as sample markets were provided for, mixing was implied. I shall now read section 10 of the order in council, the vital section giving authority:
10. Notwithstanding the provisions of the Canada Grain Act (section 229, subsection 5). to the contrary, the lessee of any special bin in any public elevator shall have the right of binning together in his special bin grain of different grades-
That is where it comes in.
-grain of different grades and the operator of any public elevator leasing any bin for special binning under these rules and regulations is hereby authorized to become the agent of the lessee to bin together in such special bin such grain of different grades received in cars for the account of the lessee, but nothing herein contained shall relieve the operator of any such public elevator of Ms liability as public warehouseman in preserving the identity of grain as binned in special bins as well as grain in public storage bins.
The meaning of the latter part, as I understand it, is that even if those mixed grades _ are _ put in a bin, their identity must be maintained just like the identity of any other grades. I hope I shall be in a position a year from now to congratulate my hon. friend on having carried out the grain act of to-day in the same spirit and with the same determination to maintain our standing abroad as has been the experience during the last few years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to try to clear
up one misapprehension under which this committee may now be labouring. The hon. member for Bow River read a statement from Hansard of yesterday. What I said was fhat I knew nothing of this except as I had been informed. My information was just as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated. Sir Josiah Stamp handed these documents over for inclusion in the report and left it to one commissioner and the secretary to determine what documents should be actually put in, and at Ottawa what did happen was that this document was included in the report.
May I draw attention to the fact that the report is not directed to His Excellency the Governor General in Council; it is directed to the Prime Minister. He would have been guilty of an offence under the criminal code had he altered a single word of the report. It was his duty to present the report to the house as he did. When I was asked why I was willing that the graph should be with-

Supply-Royal Grain Commission
drawn from the report, I answered, because it was plainly the sense of this chamber that it should be removed as the matter printed upon the graph in red ink contained propaganda. The moment my attention was directed to it I pointed out that as there was no verification of the graph it was not proper that there should be propaganda upon it and it should not be incorporated in the report. As everyone is aware, that is what would happen in a court of law. The commissioner and no one else was responsible for that particular part of it. When the graph was put in the red ink printing was on it. That was my objection to it. When it was brought to my attention after what had taken place, I realized that the proper course to follow- the sense of the house being evidenced by the statements made-was to have the graph withdrawn from the report. I said that in answer to the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray), who asked why those instructions were given. That is the explanation of the matter. Everything that I have stated is only what I have been informed. The document laid on the table was the document handed to me by the Under-Secretary of State, whose duty is was to bring it to me for that purpose. I looked only at the conclusions on the first day the report was brought to me, and I have not yet read all the details. But the report being directed to me, and not to the government, if any alterations in any way, shape or form had been made by the Prime Minister or by any other member of the government, it would have been a clear violation of the obligations laid upon them by law. The government has no responsibility in respect to the matter. The report is a report of the commission, uninfluenced and undirected by the government or by any member of it.

I do not think anybody suggested that the government ever had a right to change the report. But it was their duty to read the report, and then, if it contained any mistakes, to refer those to the commission. The very fact that a copy of the report was sent across to Sir Josiah Stamp shows that that was the proper method, and my right hon. friend knew that it was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The report was sent by
the secretary, not by the government.

Of course, that was the procedure. But the government, by their own admission, never read the report, they just took chances, and now they want to slink out of responsibility. That is their most extraordinary attitude.

The hon. member for
Bow River, speaking a moment ago, referred to certain copies of the Stamp report that had been sent to the grain exchange in Winnipeg previous to the much-talked of graph being deleted, and he suggested that the grain exchange should be requested to remove this appendix XII from the report. At the time he was speaking from memory, he had not the figures before him. Now I have the actual figures under my hand. In yesterday's Hansard at page 3239 will be found the following question by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh):
How many copies of the Stamp commission report containing appendix XII, chart, 10, were printed and distributed to the government and by whom?

Sanford Evans himself. One can easily see the reason for sending so many copies of the report to Winnipeg. Needless to say it would be quite improper for him to present the chart himself; therefore he naturally invited Mr. Pitblado, representing the Winnipeg grain interests, to do it for him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No. I think I myself did a grave injustice to Mr. Sanford Evans the other day, and quite innocently, I think, my hon. friend is doing so now. I can assure him that Mr. Sanford Evans had nothing whatever to do with the filing of the chart; it was done by Mr. Pitblado, as it belonged to his clients, the Winnipeg grain exchange.

I quite appreciate that.
Of course, we have to accept this, Mr. Chairman, that Mr. Sanford Evans was chosen by the grain interests as their representative on the commission. Although the Prime Minister, I am sure, had the very best intentions in inviting representatives of agriculture and the grain intertests to sit on the commission, I now think it was poor policy. Mr. Sanford Evans has for years been preparing such graphs. Of course, it was impossible for him to introduce this graph himself, and we know that Mr. Pitblado did introduce it as the one representing the grain interests. It was introduced at the very latest moment before the commission rose at Winnipeg. The next

The point I wish to make is that while those of us who have been in the house know very well how the minister feels about the matter, there are many members who have not been able to be here, and no notification has been sent to them through their post office boxes.

Then I should like to
ask if the minister can tell me why during January, February, March and April of this year there has been an increase of something like a million bushels of wheat shipped to Italy. I do not know whether or not the government have made any concessions to or trade arrangements with Italy, or just why Italy has increased the importation of Canadian wheat. During those four months our shipments of wheat to the British Isles remained about the same, while they showed some increase to France. I understand that France has changed its quota for two reasons. The first is that there was a poor crop; they

Supply-Canada Grain Act
had to have wheat from somewhere, and our shipments to France have increased simply because our wheat is better for mixing than any other wheat in the world. They had to bring in foreign wheat, and since they were able to buy Canadian wheat as cheaply as the wheat of any other country, we have sold something like 3,000,000 bushels more. That is not very much for four months when you consider that we have to export something like 250,000,000 bushels a year, but for all that it is a certain quantity. Can the Minister tel! us why the exportations to Italy have increased ?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As far as Italy is concerned I think the answer is obvious. In the early part of the season Italy purchased a great deal of wheat from Russia; the Russian shipments fell off during the winter months, and Italy purchased more wheat from us, which we were very glad to sell. As far as France is concerned, I think the larger quantity purchased this year is due in large measure to the visit of the Prime Minister to Paris last autumn, when he had a very interesting and very satisfactory conference with the French government.

There is no evidence whatever to that effect. Our shipments to Italy increased two and a half times, while those to France increased only one and a half times. Was the Prime Minister also interceding at Rome in connection with the sale of Canadian wheat? Without any intercession at all, apparently, the amount of wheat sales to Italy went up very much more than in the case of France, and assuming that anything was done, what did we give for it? There is not a scrap of paper or any other evidence to support my hon. friend's statement, which has been going all over this country with nothing to support it. On the other hand the proportion of foreign wheat permitted to be milled has increased from 3 per cent to 30 per cent, and France is using not only more Canadian wheat but more United States wheat as well. My hon. friend cannot support that statement at all, but if there has been any bargain made whereby we sold more wheat he should be able to rfhow what we gave in return for it and what the bargain was. There has been no attempt at all to show that. Has the French treaty been abrogated or revised? What has happened? In France they do not give things away for nothing, and the statement of my hon. friend is not supported by any facts so far as I can see.
Has my hon. friend forgotten the visit of Mr. Ferguson to Rome?

I am sorry I cannot
agree that this increase resulted from the Prime Minister's visit. We were shipping as much as 20,000,000 bushels to France in 1929, and during the four months under consideration we shipped only a little over 4,000,000 bushels. That is only at the rate of 12,000,000 bushels a year, so that 'hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be falling down on the job. Last year wte shipped 10,000,000 bushels, so our exports of wheat to France have not increased very much. We have been shipping between 12,000,000 and 20,000,00 bushels of wheat to France every year. Apparently, therefore, there has not been a very great deal of work done for the farmers of Canada. The Prime Minister is not blasting the way into very many markets for us.

I should like to make one observation, and it will interest the minister to know I am not referring to the Stamp commission or its report. I wish to refer to a statement made by the ex-Minister of Agriculture when, a few moments ago, he was urging the minister to make quite certain that the grain act, with its excellent provisions, should be administered sympathetically.
With almost all he said I am heartily in accord, but speaking of that act and of the efforts of the late government to bring it to its present state, he made use of an expression which might give a wrong impression to the committee. The ex-Minister of Agriculture stated that for a number of years the former government had been struggling with the act, but for want of an adequate majority in the house they had been unable to amend the act to bring it to its present form. As a member of one of the independent groups in the house during those years, whose presence caused a situation not very satisfactory to the late government, nor, may I add, to the late opposition, I may say that at no time would the late government have been without a perfectly safe majority in any attempt to amend the grain act to remove the objectionable features. That is the only part of the ex-minister's remarks with which I find fault. I do think, however, that the statement might leave a wrong impression among those members who were not present during those somewhat contentious years.

I am glad my hon. friend raised that question, because I had reference more particularly to what took place in the committee on agriculture. That is where the difficulty was, and the hon. member for Mackenzie, who was on the committee, knows the circumstances under which these provisions of the act were removed. I

am glad to have the opportunity of explaining that these mixing provisions, with the safeguards in the act of 1925, were eliminated because the agriculture committee mixers were stronger than the anti-mixers, and there was nothing to do but to let it go.

Lest there be further
misunderstanding, I would remind the former Minister of Agriculture that his party always had a majority on the agriculture committee. If there was any disagreement among the members of his own party, he must answer for it.

Where was the
leader of the Progressive party on that occasion, and several others also of that group?

I admit that some
members of our group, who later joined the Liberal party, did disagree with the rest of us. But apart from those two members, the group in this corner are in entire accord with the change.

Let me show how these letters came into being. Let me read the letter sent out broadcast by J. J. Gibbons Limited. This particular one is addressed to a gentleman in Aurora, Ontario, whose name I can give if it is desired. It is dated January 12, 1931, and reads:
We have had reprinted the series of letters published from October to December, 1930, by the Hon. Henry H. Stevens, Minister of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, whom we had the honour of serving as advertising agents, and thinking you might be interested we have much pleasure in enclosing you a copy of same.
We think the minister would be interested in receiving from you any comments you may feel like making on this campaign undertaken by him on behalf of the producers of Canada with a view to relieving the unemployment situation.
That letter was signed by Mr. J. J. Gibbons, the president of the company. The letters which the minister has received are communications from friends of the administration to whom Mr. Gibbons had addressed his letter. Undoubtedly, upon receiving a communication of this kind, the faithful would feel it their duty* to send the minister something laudatory of his efforts. I have no desire to stress further what is being done in connection with this campaign, but I would like to repeat it is all in the nature of protectionist propaganda and it does seem to be a grave misuse of public money for a minister of a department to spend any part of the appropriations of this parliament upon party propaganda. If I thought the minister was going to continue to do this sort of thing I would move for a reduction of the vote. My motion might fail to carry but it would draw attention to how the government has been wilfully and wastefully spending public money at a time when I think all will agree money is very much needed for far more important purposes.

Is not the
minister going to make a reply to the leader of the opposition? Does the minister think that the spending of public money is proper for this "buy in Canada" campaign?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I certainly do. I think it was a very satisfactory and successful campaign, as is evidenced by the abundance of response.

This is a matter of collective responsibility on the part of

the cabinet. Does the Minister of National Revenue approve of a campaign like this where public moneys are being spent?
He certainly does. Is that not right?
I would like to have a reply from the minister.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How does the minister arrange "Canada first" and "Empire first" campaigns to be run side by side? He has been spending $100,000 on the campaign in Canada, and he is spending public money also for the purpose of advertising in Great Britain. At a dinner of the Canadian chamber of commerce held on March 10, Mr. Ferguson said:
When I see in England such slogans as "Buy British goods made in England by British labour," it semes to me to be forgotten that the goods of Canada and other parts of the empire are equally British. Imperial consolidation cannot be effected on the lines of discrimination.
If this sort of thing-these advertisements and this creed-were distributed to the British press there would be a terrible time. The high commissioner has stated that he would resign if the government compelled him to put forward any "Canada first" ideas 'in Great Britain. He contends that he is over there to put forward "Empire first" ideas and that he will return the minute anyone tries to suppress an utterance which relates to the empire rather than to Canada.
